propositions.text: Whether retrospective changes to sentence conditions may constitute punishment violating s. 11(h) of the Charter.
Distinction between sentence imposed and conditions of sentence in criminal law.

paragraphs.summary: The court introduces the issue of whether retrospective changes to sentence conditions violate s. 11(h) of the Charter, noting the distinction between sentence and conditions.

propositions.text: Appeal arises from Parliament's conclusion that accelerated parole review (APR) was ineffective.
APR was established in 1992 as a simplified parole process for first-time non-violent offenders.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the appeal arises from Parliament's view that APR, established in 1992 for first-time non-violent offenders, was not working.

propositions.text: Canadian Criminal Justice Association criticized APR's violent recidivism test as unreliable.
APR would allow some offenders with violent records to qualify.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent cites criticism from the Canadian Criminal Justice Association that APR's violent recidivism test was unreliable and allowed offenders with violent records.

propositions.text: Despite criticism, APR was expanded in 1997 to include earlier eligibility for day parole.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes APR was expanded in 1997 to allow earlier day parole eligibility despite criticism.

propositions.text: Criticism of APR continued, including recommendations to tighten eligibility and change recidivism criteria.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent notes ongoing criticism recommending tighter APR eligibility and changes to recidivism criteria.

propositions.text: 2007 Correctional Service of Canada Review Panel found statutory and accelerated parole less effective than discretionary release.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent cites a 2007 report finding statutory and accelerated parole less effective than discretionary release.

propositions.text: Parliament repealed APR provisions via the 2011 Abolition of Early Parole Act (AEPA), effective March 28, 2011.
AEPA repeal applied retrospectively to offenders sentenced when APR was in effect, including respondents.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Parliament repealed APR retrospectively in 2011, affecting respondents sentenced when APR was active.

propositions.text: Whether retrospective delayed day parole eligibility violates respondents' s. 11(h) Charter right not to be punished twice.

paragraphs.summary: The court frames the issue whether retrospective delayed day parole eligibility violates respondents' s. 11(h) right.

propositions.text: s. 11(h) applies to respondents' claim.
Retrospective delayed day parole eligibility violated respondents' s. 11(h) right not to be punished again.
Violation was not justified under s. 1 of the Charter.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 11(h) applies, retrospective delay violated respondents' rights, and violation was not justified under s. 1.

propositions.text: No need to address respondents' s. 7 Charter claim after finding s. 11(h) violation.

paragraphs.summary: The court declines to address s. 7 claim after finding s. 11(h) violation.

propositions.text: Appeal is from BC Court of Appeal decision upholding BC Supreme Court decision in respondents' favour.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the appeal is from BC Court of Appeal upholding BC Supreme Court decisions favoring respondents.

propositions.text: Respondents were first-time, non-violent federal offenders eligible for APR at sentencing.

paragraphs.summary: The court states respondents were first-time, non-violent offenders eligible for APR at sentencing.

propositions.text: APR was automatic, paper-based, and used a lower parole release test than normal parole.
APR extended to day parole as well as full parole.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes APR as automatic, paper-based, with a lower release test, extended to day and full parole.

propositions.text: From 1997, APR day parole eligibility triggered earlier than normal parole: after one sixth of sentence or six months.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes APR day parole eligibility began earlier from 1997 than normal parole.

propositions.text: AEPA repealed APR provisions and applied repeal retrospectively to all offenders sentenced before or after repeal.
Section 10(1) of AEPA states APR does not apply as of repeal day to all offenders sentenced or transferred before, on, or after repeal day.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains AEPA repealed APR provisions retrospectively, per s. 10(1), applying to all offenders regardless of sentencing date.

propositions.text: APR repeal replaced earlier day parole eligibility with normal parole eligibility timing.
APR repeal changed parole review from automatic referral and paper review to application and hearing process.
Parole test changed from no reasonable grounds for violent offence to undue risk to society, giving Board discretion.

paragraphs.summary: The court details APR repeal effects: delayed eligibility, changed review process, and stricter parole test with Board discretion.

propositions.text: Repeal delayed respondents' day parole eligibility by 3, 9, and 21 months respectively.

paragraphs.summary: The court states repeal delayed respondents' day parole eligibility by varying months.

propositions.text: Respondents challenged constitutionality of s. 10(1) AEPA by summary trial in BC Supreme Court.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes respondents challenged s. 10(1) AEPA constitutionality in BC Supreme Court summary trial.

propositions.text: Holmes J. held s. 10(1) AEPA infringed s. 11(h) as additional punishment and was not justified under s. 1.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found s. 10(1) AEPA infringed s. 11(h) and was not justified under s. 1.

propositions.text: Holmes J. asked if APR abolition amounted to punishment violating s. 11(h).
s. 11(h) protects against additional trial or punishment after conviction or sentence (R. v. Rodgers).

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker considered if APR abolition was punishment violating s. 11(h), relying on R. v. Rodgers.

propositions.text: Punishment occurs when a consequence is part of sanctions for an offence and furthers sentencing principles, per Rodgers and Holmes J.
Delayed parole eligibility is punishment in criminal sentencing, supported by R. v. Shropshire, Chaisson, and Zinck.
Parole ineligibility from sentence or retrospective CCRA amendment is not materially different due to overlapping objectives.

paragraphs.summary: Earlier decision-maker explains punishment as sanctions furthering sentencing, finds delayed parole eligibility is punishment, and sees no material difference in parole ineligibility sources.

propositions.text: Holmes J. found s. 10(1) AEPA's purposes punitive and retrospective day parole eligibility alteration punitive in effect.
Such alteration significantly affects how offenders serve sentences.
Changes limiting parole eligibility post-sentencing are additional punishment, per Cunningham and Holmes J.

paragraphs.summary: Holmes J. found s. 10(1) AEPA punitive in purpose and effect, significantly affecting offenders, and limiting parole eligibility post-sentencing is additional punishment.

propositions.text: Holmes J. found s. 11(h) infringement not saved under s. 1 Charter despite pressing objectives.
Declared s. 10(1) invalid for retrospective application to offenders sentenced before March 28, 2011, effective immediately.

paragraphs.summary: Holmes J. found s. 11(h) infringement not justified under s.1 and declared s. 10(1) invalid retrospectively effective immediately.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal upheld trial judge, finding s. 11(h) protects against double jeopardy including sanctions after sentencing.
Retrospective legislative lengthening of jail time via delayed parole eligibility violated s. 11(h).

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal upheld trial judge, finding s. 11(h) protects against double jeopardy and retrospective parole delay violated it.

propositions.text: Levine J.A. emphasized sentencing judge and Board roles differ; judges shouldn't consider parole in sentencing.
Despite this, s. 10(1) AEPA's retrospective repeal is punishment by purpose and effect.

paragraphs.summary: Levine J.A. noted sentencing and parole roles differ but still found s. 10(1) AEPA retrospective repeal punitive.

propositions.text: s. 11(h) purpose is to prevent second punishment for an offence already tried and convicted.
Meaning of 'punishment' under s. 11(h) depends on whether consequence is part of sanctions and furthers sentencing principles per Rodgers.
Levine J.A. declined to decide s. 11(h) claim on punitive purpose alone, focusing on effect of delayed parole eligibility.
Effect of delayed parole eligibility by legislation analogous to judge-imposed delay, thus violating s. 11(h).

paragraphs.summary: Levine J.A. explained s. 11(h) prevents second punishment, focused on effect of delayed parole eligibility, finding it analogous to judge-imposed delay violating s. 11(h).

propositions.text: Court of Appeal agreed legislation responded to pressing concern but lacked evidence of minimal impairment under s. 1 Charter.

paragraphs.summary: Court of Appeal agreed legislation lacked minimal impairment evidence, so not saved under s. 1 Charter.

propositions.text: Retrospective s. 10(1) AEPA violates s. 11(h) right not to be punished again, urging broad 'punishment' reading.
Retrospective repeal eliminating early day parole eligibility is punitive in effect and purpose.

paragraphs.summary: Respondents argue retrospective s. 10(1) AEPA violates s. 11(h) by punitive effect and purpose, urging broad punishment interpretation.

propositions.text: Crown urges narrow s. 11(h) reading excluding elimination of early day parole eligibility as punishment.
Retrospective repeal aims for rehabilitation, reintegration, public safety, not punishment; effect reflects this.
s. 11(h) not engaged without duplication of criminal proceedings for same matter.

paragraphs.summary: Crown argues narrow s. 11(h) reading excludes parole elimination as punishment, aims for non-punitive goals, and requires duplication of proceedings.

propositions.text: Will first consider if s. 11(h) applies absent duplication of proceedings, then scope of 'punishment', then if provision is punishment by purpose or effect.

paragraphs.summary: Court will analyze s. 11(h) applicability without duplication, punishment scope, and if provision is punishment by purpose or effect.

propositions.text: Trial court and Court of Appeal did not address if s. 11(h) applies without duplication of proceedings.
Both courts agreed s. 11(h) protects against double jeopardy, focusing on 'punishment' meaning.

paragraphs.summary: Neither lower court addressed s. 11(h) without duplication; both agreed s. 11(h) protects against double jeopardy focusing on punishment meaning.

propositions.text: Section 11(h) states no retrial or punishment after final acquittal or conviction and punishment for offence.

paragraphs.summary: Section 11(h) prohibits retrial or punishment after final acquittal or conviction and punishment.

propositions.text: Parliament enacted s. 11(h) to protect against double jeopardy, mirroring ICCPR art. 14.7.
ICCPR art. 14.7 prohibits retrial or punishment after final conviction or acquittal.

paragraphs.summary: Parliament enacted s. 11(h) to protect against double jeopardy, mirroring ICCPR art. 14.7 prohibiting retrial or punishment after final conviction or acquittal.

propositions.text: Definition of double jeopardy is contested; Don Stuart notes complexity and need for clarification.
Double jeopardy protects against multiple trials and multiple punishments, based on fairness of proportionate punishment.

paragraphs.summary: Double jeopardy definition is contested; Stuart notes it protects against multiple trials and punishments for fairness.

propositions.text: s. 11(h) scope is narrow, with little impact on double jeopardy and double punishment protection, per Friedland and Stuart.
Broader double jeopardy interpretations may fit better under s. 7 Charter, especially for retrospective punishment issues.
Case concerns alleged punishment from retrospective legislation; s. 11(g) and s. 11(i) also address retrospectivity.

paragraphs.summary: s. 11(h) has narrow scope with little impact on double jeopardy; broader views may fit s.7; case involves retrospective punishment and related Charter provisions.

propositions.text: s. 11(h) applies to protect against punishment again after sentencing even without separate proceeding.

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes s. 11(h) protects against punishment again after sentencing even without separate proceeding.

propositions.text: Plain meaning of s. 11(h) shows protection against being tried or punished again is independent and sufficient to engage s. 11(h).
Disjunctive 'tried or punished' and conjunctive 'found guilty and punished' language clarifies s. 11(h) protection scope.
Stuart notes s. 11(h) protects against multiple trials and additional punishment harassment.

paragraphs.summary: Plain meaning of s. 11(h) protects against being tried or punished again independently, supported by Stuart's analysis.

propositions.text: Common sense supports s. 11(h) protects against punishment without trial as well as with trial.
Purpose of s. 11(h) cannot be to protect only punishment after trial but not punishment without trial.

paragraphs.summary: Common sense and purpose show s. 11(h) protects against punishment without trial as well as with trial.

propositions.text: s. 11(h) is narrow and distinct from autrefois acquit and Kienapple rule against multiple convictions.
s. 11(h) can apply to double punishment without new proceeding; no academic support for contrary view.
Some authors focus on what constitutes second proceeding for s. 11(h), but this doesn't limit s. 11(h) in double punishment without proceeding.

paragraphs.summary: s. 11(h) is narrow but applies to double punishment without new proceeding; no academic support limits this application.

propositions.text: Lack of academic commentary reflects rarity of s. 11(h) violations without second proceeding.
Early s. 11(h) cases involved criminal charges after non-criminal sanctions; question was if non-criminal sanction triggered double jeopardy.
McLachlin J. in Shubley said s. 11(h) protects against duplication in criminal proceedings, not two different proceedings from same act.
This must be read in context; protection can be triggered by criminal or true penal consequences proceedings.

paragraphs.summary: Lack of commentary shows rarity; early cases involved criminal after non-criminal sanctions; s. 11(h) protects against duplication in criminal proceedings or true penal consequences.

propositions.text: Rodgers case supports conclusion that s. 11 applies only when a person is charged with an offence, not to DNA order applications themselves
s. 11 applies to criminal proceedings for index offences, question is if s. 487.055 order is further punishment
Court rejected Crown's narrow construction of s. 11(h) limiting it to duplication of criminal proceedings
s. 11(h) protects against double punishment even without a second proceeding
Academic commentary on this issue is sparse and textbooks may need updating

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 41 explains prior case Rodgers limits s. 11 to charged persons, rejects narrow Crown view, and affirms s. 11(h) protects against double punishment without second proceeding.

propositions.text: Having concluded s. 11(h) allows double punishment claims without second proceeding, must determine if current case amounts to punishment

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 42 states court must decide if current case constitutes punishment under s. 11(h) after concluding claims without second proceeding are allowed.

propositions.text: Scope of 'punishment' under s. 11(h) has expanded over time
Criminal or quasi-criminal proceedings trigger protection against double jeopardy under s. 11(h)
Second criminal or quasi-criminal charge for same act engages s. 11(h) even if consequence is slight

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 43 explains the expanded scope of 'punishment' under s. 11(h) includes criminal or quasi-criminal proceedings even with slight consequences.

propositions.text: Wigglesworth held s. 11(h) may be triggered by non-criminal proceedings with true penal consequences
True penal consequence includes imprisonment or significant fines redressing societal wrongs, not internal discipline

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 44 cites Wigglesworth that s. 11(h) applies to non-criminal proceedings with true penal consequences like imprisonment or fines.

propositions.text: Wigglesworth found internal RCMP disciplinary proceeding involved true penal consequences due to possible imprisonment
Shubley found internal prison disciplinary sanctions lacked true penal consequences as no fines or imprisonment involved

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 45 contrasts Wigglesworth finding true penal consequences in RCMP discipline with Shubley finding no true penal consequences in prison discipline.

propositions.text: Rodgers revisited 'punishment' definition, considering DNA sample order under new legislation as potential double punishment
Charron J. accepted imprisonment and heavy fines as true penal consequences but said punishment not limited to these
Charron J. identified features of punitive sanctions including forfeiture, firearm prohibition, driving prohibition, restitution

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 46 explains Rodgers revisited punishment definition, with Charron J. expanding beyond imprisonment and fines to other punitive sanctions.

propositions.text: Rodgers two-part punishment test: sanction is punishment if part of arsenal of sanctions for offence and furthers sentencing principles
DNA order not part of criminal sanctions arsenal, does not stigmatize offender, deterrence alone not punishment
Example given: random traffic stops deter but are not punishment

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 47 states Rodgers test for punishment and finds DNA order not punishment as it lacks stigma and deterrence alone is insufficient.

propositions.text: Current case pushes limits of 'punishment' concept, requiring revisiting s. 11(h) scope
Wigglesworth and Rodgers tests do not fully address retrospective parole eligibility changes

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 48 states current case requires revisiting s. 11(h) as Wigglesworth and Rodgers tests do not address retrospective parole changes.

propositions.text: Must determine if retrospective parole eligibility changes modifying existing sanction manner constitute punishment
Alleged punishment is frustration of offender's expectations, not a second proceeding or discrete sanction

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 49 frames issue whether retrospective parole changes frustrating expectations constitute punishment, not a second proceeding or sanction.

propositions.text: Rodgers test's first branch defines punishment by traditional Criminal Code sanctions, equating sentence and sanction
Parole grant changes sentence conditions, not sentence itself (R. v. M. (C.A.))
Changes to parole system generally not part of 'arsenal of sanctions' under Rodgers test

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 50 explains Rodgers test's first branch excludes parole changes as they alter sentence conditions, not sentence itself.

propositions.text: Retrospective parole changes may extend incarceration, which is severe deprivation and core punishment
Incarceration and heavy fines are benchmark punishments under Rodgers test

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 51 notes retrospective parole changes may increase incarceration, the core punishment benchmark under Rodgers test.

propositions.text: Rodgers test is overly formalistic for parole changes, excluding many but including marginal incarceration increases
Rodgers test unsuitable for identifying functional increases in punishment from retrospective parole changes
Rodgers test designed for discrete sanctions, not modifications of original sanctions

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 52 criticizes Rodgers test as formalistic and unsuitable for retrospective parole changes increasing punishment functionally.

propositions.text: Rodgers test's second branch on sentencing principles awkward for parole changes as rehabilitation applies to both
All retrospective parole changes could be said to further sentencing principles, but not all are punitive

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 53 finds Rodgers test's second branch awkward for parole changes, as all could further sentencing principles but not all are punitive.

propositions.text: s. 11(h) precludes: (a) criminal/quasi-criminal retrial; (b) additional sanction meeting Rodgers test; (c) retrospective changes adding punishment
Current case concerns third type: retrospective repeal altering parole expectations of sentenced offenders
Not repeal itself but retrospective application alleged unconstitutional

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 54 identifies three s. 11(h) double punishment types and finds current case concerns retrospective parole changes adding punishment.

propositions.text: Charter s. 11(g) protects against retroactive criminal laws; s. 11(i) protects against harsher penalties retroactively
Peter Hogg states no general prohibition on retroactive laws except s. 11(g)
These provisions express society's repudiation of retroactive punishment broadly defined

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 55 explains Charter provisions s. 11(g) and (i) protect against retroactive criminal laws and harsher penalties, reflecting repudiation of retroactive punishment.

propositions.text: s. 11(h) protects against double jeopardy, not expressly retroactivity
Early s. 11(h) cases involved existing offences, no retroactive punishment issue
s. 11(h) may be engaged without duplication of proceedings by retrospective parole modifications increasing punishment
Non-punitive legislative changes can become punitive if applied retrospectively

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 56 states s. 11(h) protects against double jeopardy, may be engaged by retrospective parole changes increasing punishment, even if changes not punitive themselves.

propositions.text: Offenders have constitutionally protected expectations about sentence duration, not conditions
Not all parole management changes are punitive despite affecting liberty interest
Cunningham held Charter s. 7 protects only significant changes amounting to further deprivation of liberty
Trivial changes to sentence conditions do not engage s. 7 protections

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 57 explains offenders' protected expectations on sentence duration, not conditions, and s. 7 protects only significant liberty deprivations, per Cunningham.

propositions.text: Will not import Cunningham's 'substantial change' requirement into s. 11(h) context
Retrospective parole changes engaging s. 7 liberty interest may not constitute punishment under s. 11(h)
Offender has liberty expectation based on parole system at sentencing; frustrating it may engage s. 7
Cunningham: serving time on mandatory supervision offers more liberty than in prison

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 58 declines to apply Cunningham's substantial change test to s. 11(h), notes offender's liberty expectation in parole system and its frustration may engage s. 7.

propositions.text: Not all parole liberty expectations are constitutionally protected
Some retrospective parole changes may be consistent with fundamental justice despite engaging liberty interest
Line drawing needed to distinguish retrospective changes constituting new punishment under s. 11(h)

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 59 states not all parole liberty expectations are protected; some retrospective changes consistent with justice; line drawing needed for s. 11(h).

propositions.text: No universal formula for retrospective parole changes constituting punishment; context-specific
Dominant consideration is extent offender's settled liberty expectation is thwarted by retrospective law
Retrospective change automatically lengthening incarceration is clear double punishment under s. 11(h)

paragraphs.summary: Paragraph 60 holds no universal formula for retrospective parole changes; key is thwarting offender's liberty expectation; automatic incarceration lengthening is clear double punishment.

propositions.text: Sentencing judges may consider delayed parole eligibility as part of the sentence under the Criminal Code.
Delayed parole eligibility is recognized as part of punishment and sentencing policy.
Zinck prohibits considering parole eligibility in sentencing fitness assessment.
Section 743.6(1) allows courts to impose delayed parole eligibility for denunciation or deterrence.
Sentencing judges may increase parole ineligibility for second degree murder (Chaisson).
R. v. Wust states sentencing courts determine fixed parole ineligibility terms.
Shropshire notes parole ineligibility duration is the key punishment difference between first and second degree murder.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds delayed parole eligibility is part of sentencing and punishment, citing Criminal Code provisions and prior cases including Zinck, Chaisson, Wust, and Shropshire.

propositions.text: Retrospective imposition of delayed parole eligibility constitutes punishment triggering s. 11(h) protection against double punishment.
Parliament's retrospective legislation imposing delayed parole eligibility is punishment since sentencing judges may impose it for punishment.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes retrospective delayed parole eligibility is punishment and protected against by s. 11(h) because sentencing judges may impose it for punishment.

propositions.text: Whether less drastic retrospective parole changes constitute double punishment depends on case circumstances.
Retrospective changes not substantially increasing incarceration risk are generally not punitive.
Indicators of lower incarceration risk include individualized decision-making and procedural rights.
Cunningham upheld replacing automatic release with discretionary release due to procedural safeguards.
Presence of procedural safeguards is relevant to assessing punishment severity under s. 11(h).
Dominant consideration is the extent offender's settled liberty expectation is thwarted.
Extension of incarceration without regard to individual circumstances and procedural safeguards violates s. 11(h).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains that less drastic retrospective parole changes may not be punitive if procedural safeguards exist and offender's liberty expectations are respected.

propositions.text: A law may violate the Charter in purpose or effect; failing purpose test ends inquiry.
Trial judge and Court of Appeal considered purpose then effect of s. 10(1) AEPA; trial judge found violation in both.
Court of Appeal found s. 10(1) unconstitutional in effect but did not rule on purpose.
Court agrees s. 10(1) violates Charter in effect but for different reasons than Court of Appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees s. 10(1) AEPA violates the Charter in effect, noting prior courts' approaches to purpose and effect analysis.

propositions.text: Overall purpose of AEPA is not disputed and is constitutionally valid.
Court of Appeal found no serious dispute about AEPA's valid purposes including rehabilitation, public safety, and confidence in justice.
Respondents do not challenge AEPA's purposes but challenge retrospective application in s. 10(1).
Issue is the purpose of retrospective application of s. 10(1) AEPA to already sentenced offenders.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds AEPA's overall purpose valid but identifies the issue as the purpose of its retrospective application in s. 10(1).

propositions.text: Retrospective parole eligibility changes violate s. 11(h) if purpose is to prolong incarceration.
Crown argues retrospective repeal furthers rehabilitation, reintegration, public safety, and confidence goals.
Retrospective repeal applies immediately and uniformly to all offenders, including already sentenced ones.
Respondents and trial judge argue retrospective application aims at denunciation, deterrence, and punishment.
Central question is whether Parliament intended to lengthen incarceration time for already sentenced offenders.

paragraphs.summary: The court states retrospective parole changes violate s. 11(h) if intended to prolong incarceration; Crown and respondents dispute the purpose.

propositions.text: MP's statement suggests Parliament intended to extend incarceration for offenders already sentenced.
This suggests retrospective provision's purpose conflicts with s. 11(h).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes an MP's statement suggests Parliament intended to extend incarceration, conflicting with s. 11(h).

propositions.text: Despite troubling Hansard passages, court accepts Crown's articulation of Parliament's purpose.
Parole administration is distinct from sentencing.
Parliament aimed to apply normal pre-APR parole rules to all offenders, including already sentenced ones.
Applying legitimate parole objectives universally is not prima facie unconstitutional.

paragraphs.summary: The court accepts Crown's view that Parliament's purpose was legitimate parole administration applied universally, not unconstitutional.

propositions.text: Parliament's authority to modify sentence conditions is limited when modification constitutes punishment.
Legislation's effect may be unconstitutional even if purpose is legitimate.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Parliament's authority to modify sentences is limited when effects constitute punishment, despite legitimate purpose.

propositions.text: Section 10(1) AEPA deprived respondents of early day parole consideration, an expectation at sentencing.
This deprivation lengthened minimum incarceration for those qualifying under APR.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 10(1) AEPA deprived respondents of expected early day parole, lengthening incarceration.

propositions.text: Section 10(1) punished respondents again by retrospectively delaying day parole eligibility.
Effect was automatic and ignored individual circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes s. 10(1) retrospectively punished respondents by delaying parole eligibility automatically without regard to circumstances.

propositions.text: This case is a clear example of retrospective parole delay as punishment.
Shropshire confirms delayed parole eligibility is part of punishment.
Retrospective legislation imposing delayed parole triggers s. 11(h) protection against double punishment.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds this case clearly shows retrospective parole delay as punishment triggering s. 11(h) protection.

propositions.text: Formal distinction between sentencing and parole administration does not change that retrospective parole delay thwarts liberty expectations.
Legislation extending parole ineligibility under CCRA is subject to s. 11(h) scrutiny like Criminal Code provisions.
Parliament cannot avoid s. 11(h) scrutiny by amending CCRA instead of Criminal Code.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds formal distinctions do not shield retrospective parole delay from s. 11(h) scrutiny and Parliament cannot avoid it by legislative choice.

propositions.text: Constitutionality of other APR abolition aspects was not seriously argued and cannot be ruled on without full record.
Changes to review process and release criteria resemble changes upheld in Cunningham under s. 7.
Each retrospective change must be analyzed for punitive effect based on impact on liberty expectations and incarceration likelihood.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes other APR changes were not fully argued and each retrospective change requires detailed analysis for punitive effect.

propositions.text: Respondents argue s. 10(1) violates s. 7 by depriving liberty against fundamental justice principles.
Wilson J. in Gamble states accused must be tried and punished under law in force at offence time.
Having found s. 11(h) violation, court finds s. 7 decision unnecessary.

paragraphs.summary: Respondents argue s. 10(1) violates s. 7; court finds s. 11(h) violation sufficient and declines to decide s. 7 issue.

propositions.text: Court prefers addressing specific Charter guarantees over s. 7 when both pleaded.
R. v. Généreux explains s. 7 is broader but specific guarantees like s. 11(d) suffice for protection.
R. v. Pearson applies same reasoning for s. 11(e).
Section 11(h) specifically protects against retrospective delayed parole eligibility punishment; s. 7 need not be addressed.

paragraphs.summary: The court prefers specific Charter guarantees like s. 11(h) over s. 7 and declines to address s. 7 arguments here.

propositions.text: Trial judge and Court of Appeal found s. 10(1) objectives pressing and substantial but failed minimal impairment.
Court agrees s. 10(1) fails minimal impairment stage under s. 1.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with prior courts that s. 10(1) has pressing objectives but fails minimal impairment under s. 1.

propositions.text: Parliament based APR abolition on evidence that system was ineffective.
Trial judge found ensuring sentences as administered reflect court sentences is pressing and substantial objective.
Applying objectives to all offenders reflects legitimate concern for uniformity and confidence in justice.
Legislative measure including retrospective application is rationally connected to objectives.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Parliament's objectives pressing and substantial and the AEPA including retrospective application rationally connected to them.

propositions.text: Crown failed to prove no less intrusive alternative to retrospective application existed.
Uniformity is worthy but not compelling enough to justify constitutional rights deprivation.
Court of Appeal concluded sentence management objectives do not justify violating respondents' rights.
Corrections authorities have administered different parole regimes including APR for twenty years.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Crown failed to prove retrospective application was necessary and notes prior court's conclusion on rights violation.

propositions.text: Prospective repeal was available and would achieve objectives without violating s. 11(h) rights.
Retrospective application damages confidence in justice system.
Crown produced no evidence that prospective repeal would undermine objectives.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes prospective repeal was a viable alternative that would protect rights and maintain confidence, lacking Crown evidence otherwise.

propositions.text: The remedy ordered was overly broad, invalidating s. 10(1) entirely though only delay in day parole eligibility infringed rights
Offenders should benefit only from early day parole eligibility, not all abolished APR system aspects

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues the remedy was overly broad, invalidating s. 10(1) entirely though only delay in day parole eligibility infringed rights; offenders should benefit only from early day parole eligibility, not all APR aspects.

propositions.text: Both courts below held retrospective elimination of early day parole eligibility unconstitutional
No serious analysis was done on constitutionality of eliminating other APR aspects retrospectively
Punishment identified was delayed day parole eligibility, not changes to review procedure or release criteria

paragraphs.summary: Both courts below found retrospective elimination of early day parole eligibility unconstitutional but did not analyze other APR aspects; punishment was delayed day parole eligibility only.

propositions.text: Retrospective modification of review procedure and release criteria resembles sentence management changes accepted in Cunningham
McLachlin J. stated changes in how sentences are served are not contrary to fundamental justice
Legislative imposition of delayed day parole eligibility prolongs incarceration and constitutes punishment under s. 11(h)
No other AEPA aspects found unconstitutional
Pre-APR parole procedures can apply alongside early day parole eligibility timelines without impracticality

paragraphs.summary: The court finds retrospective changes to review and release resemble accepted sentence management changes; delayed day parole eligibility is punishment, other AEPA aspects not unconstitutional, and pre-APR procedures can coexist with early day parole timelines.

propositions.text: Courts below did not receive submissions on limited declaration now proposed
Court must exercise caution before departing from remedy by trial judge and Court of Appeal
Cautious approach favors upholding full declaration of invalidity

paragraphs.summary: The court notes no submissions on limited declaration were made below and concludes caution favors upholding full invalidity declaration.

propositions.text: Test for severance asks if valid part is inextricably bound to invalid part (Schachter v. Canada)
Doubts exist about respondents' claim that early day parole is functionally bound to APR scheme
Cannot presume Parliament would enact early day parole legislation without rest of APR system
Concluding early day parole is independent without evidence would overstep judicial role

paragraphs.summary: The court explains severance test, doubts early day parole is bound to APR, and cannot presume Parliament enacted it alone without evidence.

propositions.text: Even if early day parole could stand alone, severance is unworkable here
Section 119.1 depends on ss. 125 and 126 defining eligibility and terms for accelerated parole review
Section 126.1 specifies ss. 125 and 126 apply to early day parole option under s. 119.1

paragraphs.summary: The court finds severance unworkable because s. 119.1 depends on ss. 125 and 126, which define eligibility and terms for early day parole.

propositions.text: Section 10(1) AEPA repealed ss. 125, 126, 126.1 retrospectively, withdrawing early day parole rights
Section 119.1 cannot operate without ss. 125, 126, and 126.1 and is meaningless without them

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 10(1) AEPA repealed ss. 125-126.1 retrospectively, making s. 119.1 meaningless without them.

propositions.text: Reading s. 10(1) AEPA to repeal ss. 125-126.1 but not s. 119.1 is impossible to implement
Declaration of invalidity of all s. 10(1) is upheld

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes reading s. 10(1) partially as Crown proposes is impossible and upholds invalidity of all s. 10(1).

propositions.text: Appeal is dismissed and trial judge's remedy upheld
Section 10(1) AEPA violates s. 11(h) Charter and is of no force or effect
Sections 125, 126, 126.1, and by implication 119.1 CCRA continue to apply to offenders sentenced before AEPA

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the appeal, upholds the remedy, finds s. 10(1) AEPA violates s. 11(h), and that ss. 125-126.1 and 119.1 CCRA continue to apply.
